text_paragraph_1: I sometimes wonder what is ringing in the minds of some educated members and supporters of the SPLM-IG when they insist that elections are the only road to ending rebellion and violence in South Sudan. Is this an argument grounded in political feasibility, or merely in the arithmetic of retaining power?
text_paragraph_2: I do not oppose elections. I oppose reckless elections, elections conducted in a country where guns remain more trusted than institutions, where the peace agreement remains substantially unimplemented, where political space is shrinking, and where the very institutions expected to manage electoral competition have not acquired the independence and legitimacy necessary to command national confidence.
text_paragraph_3: History should make us cautious. From the violent electoral crises that accompanied Africa’s post-independence political transitions to Angola, Uganda, Kenya, Côte d’Ivoire, Burundi, Ethiopia, Zimbabwe and elsewhere, elections have sometimes become not the exit from conflict but its ignition point. In Angola, a disputed 1992 election shattered the Bicesse peace process and returned the country to devastating war. Côte d’Ivoire’s 2010 disputed presidential election produced a deadly confrontation. Kenya’s disputed elections in 1992 and 2007 exposed how electoral competition can become communal violence when institutions are weak and political identity is heavily mobilised.

Jordan’s Economy Weathers Iran War’s Shocks and Finds New Opportunities
text_paragraph_1: In the summer of 2003, King Abdullah II told Bloomberg Jordan sits “between Iraq and a hard place,” a play on words designed to describe the kingdom’s challenging environment to an American audience amid the US-led Iraq war to the east and the lingering Palestinian-Israeli conflict to the west.
text_paragraph_2: Jordan is grappling with a much “harder place” today, particularly since Hamas’ October 7, 2023, attacks on Israel, Israel’s brutal war in Gaza that has rendered vast swathes of the enclave “ uninhabitable ,” and the surging settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank. Adding to Jordan’s pressures is the mounting threat arising from the Islamic Republic of Iran’s support for militias in Iraq and drug smuggling from southern Syria. The Iran war has left the region in a perpetual state of uncertainty over the past seven months. The Iranian regime has launched more than 250 missiles and drones against Jordan — primarily targeting the US military presence as well as the port city of Aqaba, the country’s dominant trade “ gateway .” Thanks to Jordan’s strategic security partnership with the US and robust response by its armed forces, most of these projectiles were intercepted and the damage so far has been minimal. There have been no reported Jordanian casualties, but three American service members were killed. Though the physical scars of war have so far been relatively limited, the economic blows are accumulating.
text_paragraph_3: It is notable that in the aforementioned 2003 Bloomberg interview, King Abdullah contended, “We have to solve the Israeli-Palestinian issue if we really want the economies of this region to flourish and move forward.” Economic progress grounded in stability was a key priority for the Hashemite monarch then, and it is an urgent one now, as Jordan navigates the repercussions of the Iran war.

text_paragraph_1: On September 25, 2026, an event took place in Ouagadougou that almost no one outside a narrow circle of trade publications noticed: telecom regulators from Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger signed an agreement creating the Sahel Regulators Council (CRS) — a permanent body to coordinate telecom policy across the three AES states. Saïdou Pona Sankaré, head of Mali’s regulator, made no secret of the ambition: “Regulation is no longer just a technical exercise. It is an instrument of sovereignty, a lever for regional integration, and an engine of economic development.”
text_paragraph_2: On the surface, this looks like a purely bureaucratic initiative: roaming coordination, cross-border frequency management, equipment certification, consumer protection. Pasteur Poda, head of Burkina Faso’s ARCEP, listed the initial priorities almost in passing: “efficient shared roaming, cross-border frequency coordination, equipment certification, and regulation of satellite networks and emerging technologies.” It’s in that last item — “regulation of satellite networks” — that something lies buried, something none of the regional outlets that covered the event connected to the wider picture.
text_paragraph_3: Satellite infrastructure for the AES is no longer a hypothetical story, attested to by years of documented negotiations with Russia. Mali signed a memorandum with Russia’s Glavkosmos back in November 2023. In September 2024, ministers from all three AES states agreed with Roscosmos on the joint development of telecom and reconnaissance satellites. Niger went further, signing a separate agreement for three satellites. And in January 2026, Russia and Burkina Faso discussed a dedicated communications satellite for the entire AES bloc, with Russian cosmonaut Alexander Gorbunov present at the talks, which is telling in itself. Moscow doesn’t send cosmonauts to routine meetings.

Who gets to speak for Eritrea?
text_paragraph_1: Eritrea made its Miss World debut earlier this month, becoming one of the newest countries to join the competition since its founding in 1951. Miss Eritrea Snit Tewoldemedhin not only represented the country on this global platform for the first time—she won the People’s Choice Award . This achievement is a remarkable demonstration of Eritrean diaspora mobilization, but it’s not what stuck with me following the competition. In reality, the last beauty pageant I watched was probably Miss Congeniality , but as an Eritrean, it was impossible not to notice the paradox of Eritreans voting for the first time from a scattered diaspora, while those inside the country remain largely shut out of participation due to severe restrictions on internet access. It was equally impossible to overlook the irony of Miss Eritrea wearing a newspaper gown while representing a country with no freedom of the press.
text_paragraph_2: Following 30 years of struggle, Africa’s longest war for independence, Eritrea officially gained sovereignty from neighboring Ethiopia in 1993. Since then, the country has remained a one-party state with no formal elections since independence and no free press since 2001. While the world’s attention was on the September 11 attacks in the US, Eritrea shut down all independent newspapers and detained prominent dissenters, including journalists, politicians, and veteran liberation fighters. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) is presenting its 2026 International Press Freedom Award to the Eritrea 16 , marking “the 25th anniversary of the silencing of independent Eritrean media and the arrest of some of the world’s longest-detained journalists.”
text_paragraph_3: Though voices in the country are silenced, migration statistics speak louder than words. According to a 2025 report by the Migration Policy Institute , “one-third of the Eritrean-born population of about 6 million is estimated to live abroad,” citing indefinite mandatory military service, torture, and repressive humanitarian conditions as the cause for the growing exodus. Despite knowing the dangerous journey ahead, many Eritreans continue to flee across the border to neighboring Ethiopia or Sudan, and often onward toward horrific conditions in Libya, which has been the subject of many civil society protests in the European diaspora in recent weeks, including Justice for Eritreans’ September 12 protest in London .

text_paragraph_1: In a world where refugees are increasingly scapegoated and shunned by states, and where funding for refugees is shrinking, Zambia has chosen instead to include refugees into its national systems and move from a humanitarian response to a development framework. In 2023, the country launched a progressive National Refugee Policy designed to integrate refugees and foster their self-reliance. Now Zambia has built the foundations of a strong refugee model but has not created the practical conditions to fully realise it.However, laws enacted prior to the National Refugee Policy and some practical barriers continue to hamper progress and limit refugee access to work, education, and freedom of movement. Specifically, certain provisions of Zambia’s Immigration Control Act No.3 (2026) , the Constitution (2016), the Refugees Act (2017), and the Citizenship Act (2016) conflict or do not align with the National Refugee Policy. As a result refugees face significant barriers to the rights that the government has pledged to advance.
text_paragraph_2: In addition, administrative barriers persist, including permit costs. Moreover, limited funds and cuts to economic livelihood programs have stalled the transition away from encampment to one that is centered on the economic inclusion of refugees. This means the full potential and ambitions of the National Refugee Policy can not be fully realized.
text_paragraph_3: Zambia’s approach to refugees is important for the Southern African region, which hosts over 10 million forcibly displaced and stateless people. It remains both a transit country for refugees and migrants and a host country, with more than 113,000 people of concern, according to the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR). The success of Zambia’s refugee policy is important not only for Zambia and the refugees it hosts, but also to the region more broadly. For example, ongoing conflict and humanitarian crisis in the Democratic Republic of the Congo may lead to new regional refugee displacement, including into Zambia.

CSF Bus Tour gives donors firsthand look at scholarship impact. Published Oct. 9 2026. Local.
text_paragraph_1: EVERETT -- You can learn a lot about the students at St. Anthony School in Everett just by looking at the walls. Lining the hallways are posters with students' colorful self-portraits and details of their lives. They tend to agree on a lot of things. Their favorite animals are mostly dogs and cats, fast food is their favorite thing to eat, and they want to be doctors, teachers, singers, or maybe YouTubers someday. The question that prompts the most diverse answers is simply, "Where are you from?" St. Anthony's students hail from Vietnam, Ecuador, Honduras, El Salvador, Brazil, Albania, Cape Verde, Haiti, Colombia, and the Dominican Republic. Many can only attend Catholic school thanks to financial aid from the Catholic Schools Foundation (CSF), which gave out $18 million in financial aid to 4,307 students in the Archdiocese of Boston's schools this year. Forty percent of St. Anthony's 285 pre-K to eighth grade students receive CSF aid. Four years ago, enrollment had dipped below 200, threatening St. Anthony's with closure. "And then what happened?" said CSF Executive Director Mike Reardon. "There was a spurt of genius." Principal Kim Palladino, then a teacher, took the helm. CSF support of the school skyrocketed from $64,485 in FY2018 to $340,000 in FY2027. Enrollment is close to pre-pandemic levels. Almost three times as many students receive CSF scholarship funds now as before COVID.
text_paragraph_2: "The growth isn't just a number," Palladino told CSF donors at their annual Bus Tour on Sept. 30. "It represents dozens of families who have chosen Catholic education for their children." Each year, CSF supporters get the chance to relive their school days, visiting a Catholic school in the archdiocese to see where their money is going. Palladino told donors that their support "provides hope" to St. Anthony's families. "It allows parents to choose an education rooted in Gospel values," she said. "It gives children opportunities they may never have imagined." Reardon, Archdiocese of Boston Superintendent of Catholic Schools Eileen McLaughlin, CSF Chairman Emeritus Peter Lynch, and others were led through St. Anthony's by student tour guides. They saw first graders learning Spanish in Ms. Roger's class and a lesson about apples in Mrs. McCullock's preschool class. In another preschool class, it was Matthew's third birthday. He wore a paper crown for the occasion. In eighth-grade math, students were learning to calculate the angle of Yankees star Ben Rice's home runs. The guides showed Lynch the playground where they have recess, and the "water park" with fountains that cool them off in the summertime. "The teachers are very kind, and the learning is actually great," said tour guide Ellie, a fifth grader whose favorite subject is religion. Tour guide Pedro, a seventh grader, loves seeing his friends and teachers at school each day. He enjoyed getting to show the donors around. "It's honoring," he said, "very grateful that they came here and visited this beautiful school." Three of Belinda Diaz's eight children currently attend St. Anthony's. Another three are alumni. Her oldest son is considering the priesthood. In 2020, her children were enrolled in another school that closed down. Without CSF scholarships, she said, she might have been able to send one of her children to St. Anthony's, if she was lucky. Shortly after enrolling her children at St. Anthony's, her daughter was diagnosed with leukemia. "We saw how the community came together to support us, helping us not only educationally but the emotional support that they received from teachers," she said. Eighth grader Caleb Beauvoir has attended St. Anthony's since kindergarten. "I made stronger friendships and learned a lot about working together," he told donors. "The teachers at St. Anthony's are the big reason why I enjoy coming to school." They taught Caleb to be more confident, try new things, and make mistakes without fear. They taught him kindness and how to listen to others and make them feel heard. His older brothers attended St. Anthony's, as well. The oldest, David, is now a pre-law student at Suffolk University. Caleb said that wouldn't have been possible without CSF. "I am grateful for everything you have done for my family and so many of these students at St. Anthony's," he said. "Thank you for being here today, and thank you for supporting us."

text_paragraph_2: At the Somali Development Finance Forum, convened in Mogadishu on 19 September, the African Development Bank Group reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening Somalia's domestic institutions and mobilising long-term development financing. text_paragraph_3: The approach reflects a broader ambition to move from recovery-focused financing toward an economic model in which domestic enterprises and private investment play a greater role. Yet the distinction between attracting financing and generating lasting economic returns is significant. Development finance can support investment opportunities, but sustained growth requires those resources to translate into stronger production, viable enterprises and employment.

Western Sahara
text_paragraph_1: Western Sahara, a sparsely populated territory on the Atlantic coast of northwest Africa, is the site of one of the continent’s longest-running territorial disputes. The conflict dates to Spain’s withdrawal from the territory in 1975, after which Morocco and Mauritania asserted control over different parts of the former colony. They were opposed by the Polisario Front, a Sahrawi nationalist movement founded in 1973 that seeks self-determination and later established the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (SADR). Mauritania withdrew from the conflict in 1979, while Morocco ultimately consolidated control over roughly 80% of Western Sahara. The Polisario, backed principally by neighboring Algeria, administers territory east of Morocco’s fortified barrier wall and refugee camps around Tindouf in southwestern Algeria.
text_paragraph_2: A United Nations-brokered cease-fire in 1991 established the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) and envisioned a referendum on the territory’s future, but disagreements over the terms of the vote prevented it from taking place. After nearly three decades, the cease-fire broke down in 2020, although subsequent fighting has remained contained. The UN has described ongoing low-intensity hostilities , including firing incidents that create security concerns for MINURSO personnel. Diplomatically, momentum has increasingly shifted toward Morocco. The United States recognized Morocco’s sovereignty over Western Sahara in 2020 and several European countries subsequently announced support for Morocco’s autonomy plan. In October 2025, the UN Security Council went further by making Morocco’s autonomy proposal a basis for renewed negotiations, which resumed in early 2026. The territory’s final status nevertheless remains unresolved, with Morocco asserting sovereignty and the Polisario continuing to demand Sahrawi self-determination.
text_paragraph_3: A Spanish colonial possession for over half a century, Western Sahara underwent a period of decolonization from 1960 until Spain relinquished control in 1975. In the wake of World War II, the international community intensified efforts to end colonialism worldwide. Under Chapter XI of the UN Charter, colonial powers were obliged to report on “non-self-governing territories,” and Spain did so for what was then called Spanish Sahara , formally recognizing it as such in UN records. From the 1960s, the UN put increasing pressure on Spain to decolonize Western Sahara. At the time, both Morocco and Mauritania asserted territorial claims and called for integration with their respective countries during meetings of the UN Special Committee on Decolonization.
